chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid from Abu Jamilah from al-Hasan ibn Ziyad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"When a man has intercourse with his wife, and she then claims the dowry, and he says, 'I have given it to you,' then the burden of proof is upon her, and the oath is upon him." And if the matter were according to what some of our companions hold, that when he has intercourse with her, it demolishes the dowry (i.e., the full dowry becomes due or the obligation is settled), then his saying (peace be upon him) 'the burden of proof is upon her and the oath is upon him' would not have meaning, because the intercourse has already removed the right, so there is no basis for establishing proof or the oath. It is also possible that the reason in those narrations is that if he had not specified a definite dowry, but had given her something, then if the matter is thus, she has no further claim to the dowry, and what she took is her dowry. And among them is that he had not specified for her a definite dowry, which indicates what we mentioned: what al-Fudayl ibn Yasar narrated in the preceding report from his saying: 'That which she took before he had intercourse with her is that which made her private part lawful to him, and she has nothing after that.' Thus he drew attention to what we said, that he had not set for her a definite dowry.
ai.seo_question: What is the burden of proof and oath procedure when a wife claims her dowry after marital consummation?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the evidentiary burden in marital disputes, establishing that upon consummation, the wife must prove the existence of a specific dowry if the husband denies payment, while he swears an oath. The text resolves a scholarly debate by distinguishing between cases where a specific *mahr* was fixed versus those where it was not, noting that if no specific amount was agreed upon, the gifts given prior to consummation suffice as the dowry. This analysis underscores the Shia juristic emphasis on the distinction between *mahr al-mithl* (dowry of equals) and explicitly stipulated amounts in the context of marital rights.
